# Welcome! {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
## This is a draft

This handbook is a draft and still under development. Chapters may be incomplete, and content can change substantially between versions. Please email [amertens@berkeley.edu](mailto:amertens@berkeley.edu) with any questions, or if you run into trouble running the code.
:::

This handbook introduces the **Causal Roadmap**, **Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE)**, and the **Super Learner** for causal inference in epidemiology, with an emphasis on pharmacoepidemiology and clinical trial analysis. The chapters build on one another, and worked R code runs throughout.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## ▶ Run the code in your browser

Every R block in this book is also a live, editable code cell that runs entirely in the browser via [WebR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/), with no R installation required. Edit the code, re-run it, and watch the output update in place.

[**Open the interactive version →**](https://amertens.github.io/causal-learning-handbook/workshop/){.btn .btn-primary role="button"}
:::

This handbook was written by [Andrew Mertens](mailto:amertens@berkeley.edu) as part of work for the [UC Berkeley Center for Targeted Machine Learning and Causal Inference](https://ctml.berkeley.edu/), supported by a gift from Gilead Sciences. For questions, suggestions, or bug reports, please contact Andrew at [amertens@berkeley.edu](mailto:amertens@berkeley.edu).

## Who is this book for?

This handbook is written for analysts who already fit regression models in R and now need to do *causal* analysis on observational health data. That mostly means pharmacoepidemiologists, biostatisticians, and epidemiologists working on drug effectiveness, safety, and real-world evidence. The worked examples assume you are comfortable with R and basic regression. They do not assume you have seen potential-outcomes notation, targeted learning, or g-methods before.

The book is *not* a substitute for a foundational causal inference text; for that, and for other useful references, see the [Other Resources](other_resources.Rmd) page. It is meant to stand on its own for someone working through a longitudinal real-world-data analysis from scratch. The appendix includes a [Glossary](glossary.qmd) covering the abbreviations and short technical terms used throughout.

## How to use this book

**Short on time?** Start with the [Short Course](00-short-course.qmd). A single chapter covers the Causal Roadmap, TMLE (by hand and with software), and longitudinal causal inference. About an hour of reading should leave you with a working grasp of the core framework.

**Want the full treatment?** Read the handbook front to back. The chapters fall into six parts. Part I builds the conceptual foundations: why standard regression is not enough for causal questions, and how the Causal Roadmap structures an analysis. Part II works through each major estimation strategy in code. Part III moves to longitudinal settings, covering time-varying confounding, longitudinal TMLE (L-TMLE), and Longitudinal Modified Treatment Policies (LMTP). Part IV turns to diagnostics and sensitivity analysis. Part V is an end-to-end applied workflow built around the `lmtp` package. Part VI takes up special topics: effect heterogeneity, mediation, hybrid RCT/RWD designs, and time-to-event estimands. A short Synthesis part then returns to the running case study, and the appendices collect a glossary, an annotated bibliography, and external resources.

You can also jump to whatever chapter you need. Each one is self-contained enough to read on its own, though they do build on each other.

## Running Case Study

A single recurring example is used across the handbook: the longitudinal HIV antiretroviral therapy cohort from the marginal structural model literature [@vanderwal2011ipw].

| Chapter | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| [Running Case Study](00-case-study.qmd) | Clinical motivation, data structure, causal question, target trial protocol, and longitudinal DAGs. |

---

## Part I: Foundations

| Chapter | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| [Regression vs. Causal Inference](01-01-regression-vs-causal.qmd) | Why a regression coefficient for a treatment is not, on its own, a causal effect; the counterfactual ("what if everyone had been treated?") framework; and the "Table 2 fallacy", interpreting every adjusted coefficient in a regression output as a causal effect for its own variable. |
| [The Causal Roadmap](01-02-causal-roadmap.qmd) | Seven-step roadmap: target trial, causal model, estimand, identification, estimation, sensitivity analysis, and interpretation. |

---

## Part II: Core Estimators

| Chapter | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| [G-Computation](02-01-gcomputation.qmd) | Outcome modeling and standardization: fit a model for the outcome, predict each person's outcome under each treatment value, and average across the sample. |
| [IPTW](02-02-iptw.qmd) | Inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting: weight each individual by the inverse of their probability of receiving the treatment they actually got, so the weighted sample mimics one in which treatment was randomized. Covers stabilized weights, truncation, and diagnostics. |
| [Doubly Robust Estimation and TMLE](02-03-doubly-robust-tmle.qmd) | Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) and Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE): combining outcome and treatment models for double robustness. |
| [Super Learner](02-04-superlearner.qmd) | Ensemble machine learning for nuisance estimation and integration with TMLE. |

---

## Part III: Longitudinal Causal Inference

| Chapter | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| [Time-Dependent Confounding](03-07-longitudinal-td-confounding.qmd) | Why standard regression fails to address treatment-confounder feedback, and why that motivates g-methods. |
| [Longitudinal TMLE: Concepts](03-09-illustrated-ltmle.qmd) | Backwards sequential regression, targeting in the longitudinal setting, and when static regimes fail. |
| [L-TMLE By Hand](03-09b-ltmle-by-hand.qmd) | Technical companion: full by-hand implementation for two time points (optional). |
| [Adherence, Forgiveness, and Shift Methods](03-03b-adherence-shift-methods.qmd) | Comparing drugs under realistic adherence using interventions that shift the *distribution of adherence* (rather than setting adherence to a fixed value). Covers forgiveness curves, the adherence data-generating process (DGP), and four ways to shift an adherence distribution. |

## Package installations




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
## Core CRAN packages
cran_pkgs <- c(
  "tidyverse", "here", "sandwich", "lmtest", "Matrix", "survival",
  "ipw", "dagitty", "ggdag"
)

## Super Learner ecosystem
sl_pkgs <- c(
  "SuperLearner", "glmnet", "gam", "ranger", "randomForest", "xgboost"
)

## Targeted Learning and causal inference
causal_pkgs <- c(
  "tmle", "ltmle", "lmtp", "hal9001", "origami"
)

## Diagnostics and sensitivity analysis
diagnostic_pkgs <- c("EValue", "episensr", "causalsens")

## Combine and install missing packages
all_pkgs <- unique(c(cran_pkgs, sl_pkgs, causal_pkgs, diagnostic_pkgs))
installed <- rownames(installed.packages())
to_install <- setdiff(all_pkgs, installed)
if (length(to_install) > 0) {
  install.packages(to_install, dependencies = TRUE)
}
```
:::
